ABSTRACT: Conjugated allenynes serve as prominently featured
structural units in various natural products. However, the absence
of an efficient and adaptable synthesis has hindered their broader
application in synthetic endeavors and biological investigations. In
terms of atom- and step-economy, there is an urgent need for an
efficient strategy with a broader substrate scope compared to
previous reports. Herein, we report a copper-catalyzed allenic
C(sp
2
)−H alkynylation of an array of allenes with exceptional site
selectivity. While the alkynylation of aliphatic C(sp
3
)−H bonds has
been extensively studied, radical-mediated regioselective alkynylation of allenyl C(sp
2
)−H bonds via direct hydrogen atom transfer
(HAT) from the C(sp
2
)−H bond of allenes remains an unresolved challenge in synthetic chemistry. This difficulty arises from
inherent issues such as the addition of radical intermediates to allenes or alkynes and the regioselectivity of the HAT process. Our
protocol addresses these challenges and demonstrates a broader substrate scope, tolerance toward various functional groups,
including active sp
3
C−H bonds such as benzyl groups and ethers, and results in a high diversity of products.
KEYWORDS: hydrogen atom transfer, C(sp
2
)−H bond functionalization, copper catalysis, alkynylation, allenynes
■
INTRODUCTION
Conjugated allenynes are notably prominent structural units in
various natural products, underscoring their potential signifi-
cance in organic synthesis (Figure 1A).
1
Nevertheless, the
absence of an efficient and adaptable synthesis has impeded
their broader application in synthetic endeavors and biological
investigations. Consequently, significant efforts have been
directed toward developing novel methodologies for the
efficient synthesis of allenynes over the past few decades
(Figure 1B).
2
However, several issues still need to be
addressed in the development of a general strategy for
synthesizing allenynes: 1) eliminating the need for laborious
substrate synthesis processes; 2) expanding the substrate scope
to enable the synthesis of various allenynes; 3) reducing
reaction susceptibility; 4) enhancing reaction atom- and step-
economy.
Alkynes represent ubiquitous functional groups with high
synthetic versatility, often found in drugs, natural products, and
organic materials.
3
Recent advancements in radical chemistry
have propelled the chemistry of alkynes forward, sparking
considerable interest in methods for selectively introducing
alkynes into organic molecules.
4
Direct alkynylation of
aliphatic C(sp
3
)−H bonds has emerged as a popular and
efficient approach for synthesizing substituted alkynes (Figure
1C).
5
However, the direct alkynylation of more challenging
C(sp
2
)−H bonds remains relatively underdeveloped (Figure
1D).
Direct insertion of a functional group into a molecule
through C−H bond functionalization stands as one of the most
extensively investigated approaches in organic synthetic
chemistry.
6
Given the prevalence of C−H bonds in organic
molecules, this method offers access to desired products with
improved atom- and step-economy compared to classical
synthetic methods. Consequently, C−H bond functionaliza-
tion serves as a potent tool for enhancing synthetic efficiency,
particularly in medicinal chemistry, natural product synthesis,
and the production of bioactive compounds. To tackle this
formidable task, one of the most promising concepts involves
the homolytic cleavage of C−H bonds via hydrogen atom
transfer (HAT) processes.
7
Significant progress has been
achieved in the functionalization of aliphatic C(sp
3
)−H bonds
through radical HAT processes. However, only a few examples
of allenyl C(sp
2
)−H functionalization have been reported,
typically involving sequential C�C addition/C−H cleavage or
concerted C�C activation/C−H deprotonation followed by

11
This strategy involves the abstraction of a hydrogen
atom from the sp
2
-hybridized carbon atom by a reactive
nitrogen-centered radical, resulting in the formation of a
diffusible allenyl radical.
Motivated by these studies, we hypothesized that direct
alkynylation of allene C−H bonds would represent an atom-
and step-economic strategy for synthesizing allenynes under
mild conditions, without the need for intricate substrates
synthesis process or harsh reaction conditions. The greater
efficiency of overlap between the π bond and the orbital of the
single electron
12
(Figure 1D, right) suggests that the linear
structure of the allenyl radical is thermodynamically more
stable than the vinyl radical, resulting in the relatively lower
BDE (∼88 kcal/mol) of the allene C(sp
2
)−H bond. However,
several challenging issues must be addressed to realize allene
C(sp
2
)−H alkynylation: (1) Both allenes and alkynes in the
starting materials and products are highly reactive in radical
reactions due to their π system, making them prone to undergo
radical addition to the C−C π bond; (2) Controlling site-
selectivity during the hydrogen atom abstraction (HAA)
process in the presence of both the allenyl C−H bond and
other reactive C(sp
3
)−H bonds is essential. Therefore, in this
study, we utilize copper salt as a catalyst and N-fluoro-N-
alkylsulfonamide as an HAT reagent
13
to achieve the direct
alkynylation of allene C−H bonds under mild conditions. This
approach yields good yields and exclusive selectivities (Figure
1D).
■
RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
A trisubstituted allene (1a) containing an allenyl C−H bond
and two formal allyl C−H bonds, which could potentially
compete in the hydrogen atom abstraction (HAA) process,
was subjected to screening of reaction parameters (for more
details, see Supporting Information). The initial experiment
involved screening alkynylated reagents using CuI as the
catalyst and 4,4′-ditert-butyl-2,2′-dipyridyl (dtbbpy) as the
ligand. The reaction with trimethylsilylacetylene (I) yielded
the desired allenyne (3a), albeit with a low yield (Table 1,
Entry 1). However, when replacing alkyne (I) with phenyl-
acetylene (II), the reaction failed to produce the correspond-
ing product (Table 1, Entry 2). Interestingly, the reaction using
disilyl-substituted acetylene (III) proceeded smoothly to yield
the desired product (3a) with an excellent yield and perfect
regioselectivity (Table 1, Entry 3), wherein C−Si cleavage
occurred on the silyl ether (Si(OMe)
3
) side rather than
trimethylsilyl group (TMS). The selectivity of C−Si scission
will be discussed in mechanistic studies.
14
The optimized reaction conditions for regioselective
alkynylation of allene C−H bonds were employed to
investigate the generality of our protocol (Scheme 1). First,
the substrate scope of trisubstituted allenes was examined. A
variety of allenes bearing either electron-donating or electron-
withdrawing aryl groups were found to be suitable substrates,
affording the products (3a−3l) in moderate to excellent yields
with good regioselectivities. Allene derivatives (1m or 1n) with
long pendant aliphatic chains also reacted efficiently to provide
the corresponding alkynylated products (3m or 3n). Addi-
tionally, allenes bearing with cyclopropyl, 3,4-dihydro-(1H)-
benzopyranyl, and tetrahydronaphthyl groups were readily
converted into the desired alkynylated compounds (3o−3q).
Notably, in the case of 3o, no “radical clock” process-driven
ring-opening product derived from the propargylic radical, a
resonance structure of the allenic radical, was detected. It is
worth mentioning that the presence of ether (3p) or benzylic

This protocol exhibited excellent tolerance toward various
structural units, including cyclohexane (3w), decane (3y),
iodine (3z), and ester (3ac). Notably, the allenic C−H bond
(1x) adjacent to a cyclopropyl ring underwent alkynylation
readily without forming any ring-opening products via the

3

(3ab), and unprotected alcohol (3ad), remained intact under
these conditions. The reaction with 1,3-diaryl allene success-

yield likely due to high steric hindrance. Additionally,
naphthyl-substituted were well-tolerated, leading to the
formation of the corresponding product (3af) in synthetically
useful yields. Remarkably, besides aryl-substituted allenes,
allene substrate (1ag) bearing an alkyl group was also
amenable to our protocol, affording the desired allenyne
(3ag) with excellent regioselectivity. Next, the compatibility of
disubstituted allenes with two allenic C(sp
2
)−H bonds, which
might compete in the HAA process (Scheme 1, bottom), was
explored. Disubstituted allenes substituted with ortho- and
para-halogenated aryl groups smoothly underwent site-specific
HAT from the allenyl C−H bonds near the aliphatic chain
with less steric hindrance. This led to a series of trisubstituted
allenes (3ah−3al) with synthetically useful yields and excellent
regioselectivities.
Subsequently, the scope of the alkynyl moiety of silyl ethers
was examined with 1d (Scheme 2). Both phenyl and alkyl
alkynes could be readily incorporated into the allene scaffold,
leading to corresponding allenynes (3ba−3be) with excellent
regioselectivities. Of note, the highly reactive ether C(sp
3
)−H
bonds in both the alkynylated reagent (2d) and the product
(3bd) remained intact in this HAT protocol.
The scaled-up preparation of 1a proceeded readily and
delivered a comparable yield, demonstrating the practicality of
the protocol (Scheme 3A). The products can be conveniently
transformed into other valuable compounds (Scheme 3B). For

generated bromo-1,3-diene (4) through C−H bond elimi-

A radical-clock experiment was designed to detect the allenyl
radical (Scheme 4A), and the desired ring-opening product
(12) was obtained. These results confirmed the formation of
the allenyl radical in the transformation. We also conducted
radical trapping experiments using TEMPO and BHT
(Scheme 4B). Under standard conditions, the addition of
two equivalents of each trapping agent resulted in complete
inhibition of the reaction. Additionally, possible trapping
compounds, 10 and 10’, were detected by mass spectrometry.
Hammett plots suggest that the electronic properties of the
aryl group on the allenes did not significantly influence the
reaction efficiency, thereby potentially excluding an ionic
reaction mode (Scheme 4C).

Based on previous reports and mechanistic studies, we
propose a plausible pathway (Scheme 5). The interaction
between Cu(I) and the HAT reagent forms a Cu(II)-bound N-
centered radical (NCR). This Cu-complex-bound NCR
species selectively abstracts a hydrogen atom from the allene
C(sp
2
)−H bond to generate the allenyl radical (A).
15
The
interaction between the Cu(II)F complex and the alkynylating
reagent yields a Cu(II)-alkyne species (B), which, upon
interception by A, forms C. The subsequent reductive
elimination of C yields the final product (3) and regenerates
Cu(I) to continue the catalytic cycle.
■
CONCLUSION
In summary, we have presented a novel copper-catalyzed, site-
selective radical alkynylation of allenyl C(sp
2
−H bonds under
mild conditions. This method affords a range of valuable
functionalized allenyne derivatives in synthetically useful yields.
DFT calculations offer theoretical insights into chemo-/regio-
selectivity of HAT process and the crucial role of the silylether
moiety as a removal group in the alkynylating reagent. The
approach demonstrates a broader substrate scope, tolerance
toward various functional groups, and yields high product
diversity.
